summary: Specifies using Digital Transmission Content Protection (DTCP) certificates as an authorization data type in the TLS authorization extension, following the guidelines in RFC 5878. It lets devices show DTCP credentials as part of a TLS handshake.

plainLanguage.summary: A secure chat that also asks for a special membership card. This explains how to show a content-protection membership card during setup.

questions: how does tls authorization data work
subtitle: How a TV or set-top box can show its content-protection certificate during a TLS handshake.

tldr.problem: Many consumer electronics devices hold DTCP certificates issued by DTLA, but there was no standard way to present them to a web service during a TLS handshake.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers a new TLS authorization data type, dtcp_authorization(66). A server sends a 32-byte random nonce, and the client answers with its DTCP certificate and a signature made with the certificate's private key, carried in the SupplementalData handshake message.
tldr.outcome: A server can learn which DTCP-certified device it is talking to, for example to verify supported features. What the server then does with that is outside the RFC's scope.

today: RFC 7562 is an Informational Independent Submission, so it is not an Internet Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Why DTCP Certificates in TLS
sections.content:
RFC 5878 lets TLS carry authorization information between client and server before any protected data flows. This RFC, an Independent Submission, uses that machinery for Digital Transmission Content Protection (DTCP) certificates issued by the Digital Transmission Licensing Administrator (DTLA).

The RFC says a substantial number of deployed devices, such as televisions, tablets, game consoles and set-top boxes, already contain these certificates. They are normally used to move premium audiovisual content between devices, but they can also verify device functionality, such as supported features. The goal here is to let web services use them that way, for example web applications on televisions.

The actual authorization decision made by the client or server is beyond the scope of the document. The DTCP certificate is not an X.509 certificate, but it can be tied to the X.509 certificate used for the TLS session by an EC-DSA signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of TVs already carry a special ID card for protecting movies. This RFC lets a TV show that card to a website when they start talking securely.

sections.title: The Building Blocks
sections.content:
DTCP certificates come in three variations: Format 0 (Restricted Authentication, for devices with limited computation resources), Format 1 (Baseline Full Authentication, the most commonly issued) and Format 2 (Extended Full Authentication, for devices with additional functions). Only Formats 1 and 2 may be exchanged here, because the mechanism needs the EC-DSA private key that goes with the certificate.

Two existing TLS pieces are reused. RFC 4680 defines the SupplementalData handshake message. RFC 5878 defines the client_authz (7) and server_authz (8) extension types, which a hello message uses to say it will send or receive authorization data in SupplementalData messages. It also sets up an IANA registry of authorization data formats, and this RFC adds one more format to it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of cards, but only the two that come with a secret key can be used. TLS already has a slot where extra papers can be handed over, so the card goes in that slot.

sections.title: The DTCP Authorization Data
sections.content:
The new type is dtcp_authorization(66). When it is in use, the authorization data is a dtcp_authz_data structure with four parts: a nonce, a DTCPCert, an ASN.1Cert and a signature.

  • The RandomNonce is 32 bytes from a high-quality, secure random number generator. The server generates it, and the client always sends it back. It helps the server detect replay attacks.
  • DTCPCert is the sender's DTCP certificate.
  • ASN.1Cert is the certificate used to establish the TLS session. If it is not sent, its length MUST be zero.
  • The signature covers the nonce, the DTCP certificate and the ASN.1 certificate if present. It is made with the private key of the DTCP certificate, proving the sender holds it. A sender sending its own DTCP certificate MUST populate it.

The signature length depends on the algorithms chosen in the DTCP specification, so it is not encoded explicitly. The RFC gives 40 bytes for a SHA1+ECDSA combination as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: The message holds a random number the server made up, the TV's card, the TV's regular secure ID, and a signature. The signature shows the TV really owns the card and is not just repeating an old message.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
To ask for this exchange, a client puts both client_authz and server_authz in its ClientHello, with the dtcp_authorization format in the extension data. A server that agrees answers with both extensions in its ServerHello. If the client did not offer both extensions with this type, the server MUST NOT include support for it.

The server speaks first in SupplementalData. It MUST generate and fill in the RandomNonce, because it cannot know yet whether the client will send an X.509 certificate. A server MAY include its own DTCP certificate; if it does not, it sends only the nonce. If it does include one, it MUST also include its server certificate, tying the data to the TLS session and helping the client detect replay.

The client then sends back the same nonce. Clients MUST include their DTCP certificate, and MAY include their ASN.1 certificate to bind the data to the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The website hands over a random number first. The TV then sends back that number plus its card and signature, so the website knows the answer is fresh.

sections.title: Alerts and IANA Registration
sections.content:
Errors reuse existing TLS alerts. A client sends unsupported_extension, always fatal, when a ServerHello supports dtcp_authorization in only one of client_authz and server_authz. Leaving the extensions out entirely is allowed and is not a reason for this alert. Either side sends certificate_unknown when an X.509 certificate inside the authorization data does not match the one sent in the Certificate or ClientCertificate message.

The IANA "TLS Authorization Data Formats" registry gets the entry dtcp_authorization(66), assigned by Specification Required under RFC 5226. The extension is compatible with DTLS, and the registry entry is marked "Y" for DTLS-OK.
sections.plainLanguage: If the two sides disagree about the rules or the papers do not match, TLS has ready-made warning messages to stop the chat.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data identifies the device, and including the X.509 certificate lets an application tie the two together. But a TLS client need not have an X.509 certificate. Then the exchange is prone to a man-in-the-middle attack, and a server MUST deny access to features that depend on the DTCP certificate, or use a double handshake.

The double handshake is itself open to the TLS renegotiation attack, so clients and servers MUST use the secure_renegotiation extension from RFC 5746. Servers MUST also use the same ASN.1 certificate in renegotiation as in the first handshake, to mitigate the Triple Handshake exploit. Extensions such as session tickets that change the handshake sequence may break the SupplementalData exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: If the TV has no regular secure ID, someone could sneak in the middle and pretend. In that case the website must hold back the special features or do the handshake twice with extra safety rules.
